analysis.title: Strategy Matters: Why Europe's Earnings Defy Its Economy
key_insights: GS raises its STOXX 600 EPS growth forecasts to 18% for 2026 (from 15%) and 7% for 2027 (from 5%), and introduces a 2028 forecast of 5%. The upgrade comes from an updated earnings framework with direct contributions from Financials and Commodities.

GS forecasts sit slightly below bottom-up analyst consensus, which expects EPS growth of more than 20% in 2026, 9% in 2027 and c.10% in 2028. Excluding Commodities, consensus expects 15% in 2026 and 12% in 2027, and the median company is expected to grow around 10% in both years.
Over the past year earnings growth has been the principal driver of European equity returns. It let the market absorb higher bond yields, renewed energy pressures and subdued domestic growth.

The earnings-GDP gap has widened. In 2025 Euro area nominal GDP grew around 3.7% against STOXX 600 EPS growth of 2.4%. GS economists expect nominal GDP growth of 3.3% in 2026 and 2.8% in 2027, well below the pace of earnings growth.

Sector mix explains part of the gap. Financials are 33% of EURO STOXX earnings but 10% of Euro area gross value added, Energy is 9% of earnings with almost no direct weight in the economy, and Technology is 11% of earnings and 4% of activity. Industrials, Real Estate and Retail are c.45% of the economy but 15% of listed earnings.
Earnings weight minus economy weight is above +20pp for Financials, +9pp for Energy and +7pp for Technology. It is -13pp for Real Estate, -10pp for Retail and -8pp for Industrials.

Geographic mix is the second factor. The Euro area share of STOXX 600 sales fell from more than 60% in 1990 to about one-third today, and more than half of revenues are earned outside Europe. Sales-weighted real GDP growth has exceeded Euro area real GDP growth in most years since the early 2000s.

The model estimates that a 1pp rise in sales-weighted GDP growth is associated with around 10pp higher STOXX 600 EPS growth. GS expects sales-weighted real GDP growth of 2.2% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027, which adds about 1pp to 2027 EPS growth, all else equal.

FX links international activity to reported earnings. A weaker euro raises the translated value of overseas profits and the competitiveness of European companies, since a meaningful share of revenues is in US dollars.

An energy shock can hurt the economy without hurting earnings. Europe is a net energy importer, but the oil intensity of GDP has fallen and the market's composition cushions the effect. Energy and Basic Resources benefit directly, while Chemicals and many Industrials pass higher costs through to customers.

Margin risk outside Energy is the main caveat. After the 2022 energy shock, Energy earnings rose quickly, and 6-12 months later Energy and Chemicals estimates began to fall as commodity prices normalised and cost pressure showed up. GS says the Middle East shock could follow a similar sequence, with margins outside Financials and Commodities coming under pressure if demand slows and pricing power fades.

Margins are where GS differs most from consensus. For the STOXX 600 excluding Financials and Commodities, GS forecasts broadly flat margins through 2028, while consensus expects more than 100bp of expansion, from around 8.7% to 10.1%. At 8.7% in 2026E margins are already close to an all-time high.

GS lists AI-related productivity gains as an upside risk to margins, though some of the benefit may be passed to consumers. Higher refinancing costs and persistently elevated energy prices are the downside risks.

Forecast assumptions: stable global growth, flat margins, Brent averaging US$88/bbl in 2027 and US$73/bbl in 2028, and a firmer copper assumption. Energy earnings fall as oil declines, only partly offset by Basic Resources.

Higher core inflation tends to support sales growth, but whether it lifts earnings depends on pricing power and margins. The higher-rate environment that accompanies inflation can support parts of Financials.
Europe-US comparison: GS sees STOXX 600 EPS growth slowing from 18% in 2026 to 7% in 2027 and S&P 500 growth slowing from 36% to 11%. The US still grows faster, but the gap narrows in 2027.

Technology is 43% of S&P 500 earnings but 7% of STOXX 600 earnings, so the US index captures more of the AI investment cycle. The ten largest S&P 500 companies produce 40% of index earnings against 19% for the ten largest STOXX 600 companies, and about 30 STOXX 600 companies are needed to reach 40%. In 2019 the figures were 23% and 20%.
earnings_insights: GS forecast (not a print): STOXX 600 EPS growth of 18% in 2026, 7% in 2027, 5% in 2028. Prior GS forecasts were 15% for 2026 and 5% for 2027.
Bottom-up consensus (estimate): STOXX 600 EPS growth of more than 20% in 2026, 9% in 2027 and c.10% in 2028. The FactSet consensus in Exhibit 12 is 23.2% for 2026 and 8.4% for 2027.
Consensus estimate excluding Commodities: 15% EPS growth in 2026 and 12% in 2027, with the median company at around 10% in both years.

Realised 2025 STOXX 600 EPS growth was 2.4%. GS 2026E/2027E by group (forecast, consensus in brackets): ex Financials and Commodities 8.7%/6.5% (16.2%/12.6%), Financials 14.3%/11.0% (12.0%/11.1%), Commodities 90.1%/-0.3% (107.5%/-11.1%).
GS margin forecast ex Financials and Commodities is broadly flat through 2028 at about 8.7% (2026E), against a consensus estimate of expansion to 10.1%.
GS top-down estimates for S&P 500 EPS growth are 36% in 2026 and 11% in 2027, against STOXX 600 at 18% and 7%. These are forecasts.

macro_indicators.interpretation: GS economists' estimate, well below the 18% STOXX 600 EPS growth forecast, which shows earnings decoupling from domestic activity.
GS economists' estimate, still well below the 7% EPS growth forecast for 2027.
Last year GDP and earnings were broadly aligned, with STOXX 600 EPS growth at 2.4%.
Little acceleration. The model translates the 2027 pickup into about 1pp of additional EPS growth, all else equal.
Falling oil reduces Energy sector earnings, only partly offset by Basic Resources on a firmer copper assumption.

risk_factors: Margins outside Financials and Commodities could come under pressure if demand slows and pricing power fades, as input costs rose and pricing power faded in 2022-2023.
Persistently elevated energy prices are a downside risk to margins and to the modest growth contribution from sales-weighted GDP.
Higher refinancing costs are a downside risk to margins.
The commodity rebound fades in 2027 and 2028 as oil declines, removing a large contributor to headline EPS growth.
Global growth does not accelerate, which limits both EPS growth and margin expansion.
Upside risk to GS margins: AI-related productivity gains, although some may be passed on to consumers in a competitive environment.
charts_described: Exhibit 1 plots annual STOXX 600 EPS growth since 1990 with GS forecasts of 18% (2026), 7% (2027) and 5% (2028) against a dashed 6.4% historical average.
Exhibit 2 compares sector shares of Euro area gross value added with EURO STOXX earnings and market cap weights, e.g. Financials 10% / 33% / 24% and Real Estate 14% / 1% / 1%.
Exhibit 8 shows STOXX 600 sector 2026 EPS revisions since the start of the Middle East conflict, with annotations Energy +112%, Travel and Leisure -21% and Autos & Parts -36%.
Exhibit 12 tabulates realised 2025 and GS 2026E/2027E EPS growth against FactSet consensus for STOXX 600, Financials, Commodities and the ex Financials and Commodities group.
Exhibit 13 compares GS 2026 and 2027 EPS growth for S&P 500 (36%, 11%) and STOXX 600 (18%, 7%).
Exhibit 15 lists the top 10 companies by earnings weight, totalling 40% for the S&P 500 and 19% for the STOXX 600.
geopolitical: Middle East conflict and the resulting energy shock: Energy sector 2026 EPS revisions have been strongly positive since the conflict began, while higher energy prices squeeze European households and corporate costs. GS says the shock could follow the 2022-2023 sequence.

tension_points.bull_case: Consensus expects margins ex Financials and Commodities to expand by more than 100bp, from around 8.7% to 10.1%. GS also names AI-related productivity gains as an upside risk.
tension_points.bear_case: GS forecasts broadly flat margins through 2028. Margins are driven by changes in growth momentum, which GS expects to stay stable, and 8.7% is already close to an all-time high. Higher refinancing costs and elevated energy prices are further downside risks.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Margins would expand only if sales-weighted GDP growth accelerates, which GS does not expect (2.2% in 2026, 2.3% in 2027, 2.4% in 2028). In the 2022 episode, Energy and Chemicals estimates began falling 6-12 months after the shock.

tension_points.bull_case: Energy and Basic Resources benefit directly from higher commodity prices, and Chemicals and many Industrials pass higher costs through. Energy sector 2026 EPS revisions are strongly positive since the Middle East conflict began.
tension_points.bear_case: Europe is a net energy importer, so higher prices squeeze household purchasing power and corporate costs. Margins outside Financials and Commodities could weaken if demand slows and pricing power fades.
tension_points.what_invalidates: GS assumes Brent averages US$88/bbl in 2027 and US$73/bbl in 2028, so Energy earnings fall as oil declines and the commodity contribution to EPS growth fades.

theme_stances.key_argument: Sector mix and revenue earned outside Europe let STOXX 600 earnings grow far faster than Euro area GDP.
theme_stances.evidence: global rather than domestic growth is increasingly more relevant for listed companies

theme_stances.key_argument: GS forecasts flat margins outside Financials and Commodities because growth momentum is not expected to accelerate, while consensus expects expansion.
theme_stances.evidence: Margins are where we differ most from consensus

theme_stances.key_argument: Higher energy prices lift Energy and Basic Resources earnings even as they weigh on the economy, but margin pressure elsewhere may follow with a lag.
theme_stances.evidence: An energy shock can be bad for the economy without being bad for earnings.
